Let ${J}_{n}(\lambda )$ denote an $n\times n$ Jordan block with $\lambda $ on the main diagonal. Fill in the missing entries in the matrix below.
$\operatorname{sin}⁡(3{J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{6}))=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

In this case, we have $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡3x,$ $n=2,$ and $\lambda =\frac{\pi }{6}.$

Since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first $2-1=1$ derivative of $f:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡3x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(\frac{\pi }{6})) & =[\begin{aligned}f(\frac{\pi }{6}) & {f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\ 0 & f(\frac{\pi }{6})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) & 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ 0 & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
E=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{6} & 0 \\ \frac{5\pi }{6} & \pi \end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\pi }{6} & 0 \\ 0 & \pi \end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $E=PD{P}^{-1},$ find $4\operatorname{sin}⁡E.$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and matrices $A$ and $S,$ where $S$ is invertible, we have

$$
f(SA{S}^{-1})=S\cdot f(A)\cdot {S}^{-1}.
$$

For $f(x)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡E$ and the given matrix $C,$ we have

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡E=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(PD{P}^{-1})=P\cdot (4\operatorname{sin}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1}.
$$

Now, since $D$ is a diagonal matrix, we get

$$
4\operatorname{sin}⁡D=[\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{6} & 0 \\ 0 & 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi \end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Also, the inverse of $P$ is

$$
{P}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}4\operatorname{sin}⁡E & =P\cdot (4\operatorname{sin}⁡D)\cdot {P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

| $\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2))=\,\,$ |  | $0$ | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |
|  |  | $0$ | $0$ | {{field-5}} |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡([\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(2) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(2)\end{aligned}]) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)) & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2))\end{aligned}] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2))\,⊕\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2)).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{2}(2),$ we have $n=2$ and $\lambda =2.$ \since $n=2,$ we need to compute the first derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{2}(2)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(2) & {f}^{′}(2) \\ 0 & f(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(2),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ \since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(2)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{2}(2))\,⊕\,\operatorname{ln}⁡({J}_{1}(2)) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡2 & \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a function $f$ and a Jordan block ${J}_{n}(\lambda ),$ we have

$$
f({J}_{n}(\lambda ))=[\begin{aligned}f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & \frac{{f}^{″}(\lambda )}{2!} & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-1)}(\lambda )}{(n-1)!} \\ 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) & ⋯ & \frac{{f}^{(n-2)}(\lambda )}{(n-2)!} \\ ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ 0 & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda ) & {f}^{′}(\lambda ) \\ 0 & ⋯ & ⋯ & 0 & f(\lambda )\end{aligned}].
$$

First, note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2({J}_{3}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2))} & ={3}^{([\begin{aligned}{J}_{3}(1) & 0 \\ 0 & {J}_{1}(2)\end{aligned}])} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{({J}_{3}(1))} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{({J}_{1}(2))}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={3}^{({J}_{3}(1))}\,⊕\,{3}^{({J}_{1}(2))}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we compute the function of each Jordan block separately.

- For ${J}_{3}(1),$ we have $n=3$ and $\lambda =2.$ Since $n=3,$ we need to compute the first and second derivative of $f$ only:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={3}^{x} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & ={3}^{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & ={3}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{3}(1)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) & \frac{1}{2!}{f}^{″}(1) \\ 0 & f(1) & {f}^{′}(1) \\ 0 & 0 & f(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{1} & {3}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & \frac{1}{2}\cdot {3}^{1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)^{2} \\ 0 & {3}^{1} & {3}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ 0 & 0 & {3}^{1}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & \frac{3}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)^{2} \\ 0 & 3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${J}_{1}(2),$ we have $n=1$ and $\lambda =1.$ since $n=1,$ we don't need any derivatives. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f({J}_{1}(2)) & =[\begin{aligned}f(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{3}^{(2)}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{({J}_{3}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2))} & ={3}^{({J}_{3}(1))}\,⊕\,{3}^{({J}_{1}(2))} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & \frac{3}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡3)^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 3\operatorname{ln}⁡3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
